question: to the Commission César Luena (S&D) Subject:

According to various studies, Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364 on the first phase of the establishment of a common Union rating scheme for data centre included a general confidentiality clause, ‘copied word for word’ from a proposal submitted by Microsoft, which obliges the Commission and Member States to keep the indicators and information for each individual data centre confidential, limiting disclosures to aggregated data1. The experts cited warn that this ‘broad presumption of confidentiality’ could run counter to the requirements for access to environmental information laid down in the Aarhus Convention, Directive 2003/4/EC and Regulations (EC) No 1367/2006 and (EU) 2021/1767. Can the Commission therefore say: 1.

How it can ensure that this clause is compatible with the aforementioned rules, stipulating as they do that exceptions on the grounds of business secrecy may only be granted under strict interpretations of the rules and cannot be invoked to deny access to information relating to emissions into the environment?
Why it has opted for automatic confidentiality rather than a case-by-case assessments when deciding whether to publish, at the very least, the information essential for assessing local impacts?
Whether it intends to review this clause in light of the forthcoming energy efficiency package for data centres to ensure reliability and prevent greenwashing?
Investigate Europe. How Big Tech wrote secrecy into EU law to hide data centres’ environmental toll, 16 April 2026.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.8.2026) The Energy Efficiency Directive (EED)1 requires the Commission to establish a European database on data centres with data publicly available on an aggregated level. The Commission established the European database2 in line with these provisions and has fulfilled its obligation to make publicly available aggregated data via a public dashboard3 that summarises and presents data as soon as they are confirmed by the Member States. The Commission has repeatedly confirmed4 that the confidentiality of the data in the European database is compatible with EU law, as well as the provisions of the Aarhus convention. To increase transparency, the Commission has committed to analysing every year the figures reported to the European database. The analysis for the first year is publicly available5 and the analysis for the second year is being prepared. Member States and not the Commission decide which specific data, data centres in their territory must publish. The Commission, as part of the EED transposition check, is examining whether Member States have transposed and implemented the relevant provisions of the Directive correctly. Similarly, Member States’ authorities can decide, during the permitting or possible local consultation processes, what information they want to disclose about the benefits and impacts of new data centres at the local level. The upcoming Data Centre Energy Efficiency Package is not foreseen to review the EED.
1 Directive (EU) 2023/1791 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 September 2023 on energy

efficiency and amending Regulation (EU) 2023/955 (recast) (OJ L 231, 20.9.2023, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2023/1791/oj). 2 Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364 of 14 March 2024 on the first phase of the establishment of a common Union rating scheme for data centres, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_del/2024/1364/oj. 3 https://dashboard.tech.ec.europa.eu/qs_digit_dashboard_mt/public/sense/app/940a61c3-bcfe-47d6-a78625d93aa63b85/sheet/ZLWpJa/state/analysis/bookmark/381456a5-1044-4047-92f5-671be7ad92c4. 4 For example, in this confirmatory request: https://ec.europa.eu/transparency/documentsrequest/search/document-details/18424. 5 https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/83be4c3e-5c79-11f0-a9d0-01aa75ed71a1/language-en.
